blocks.text: On this bird see Aelian, Hist. Animal. book 3, ch. 42; Pliny, Hist. Nat. book 10, ch. 46. It is the Fulica porphyrio of Linnaeus (vol. 1, part 2, p. 699, ed. Gmelin), with red forehead, many bracelets, a green body violet beneath; in French Poul-Sultane. To Oedmann the πορφυριων [porphyriōn] of the Greeks seems to be the Phoenicopterus ruber of Linnaeus (vol. 1, part 2, p. 612) (Vermischte Sammlungen, 3, p. 57), but he does not add reasons for his opinion.
Otus of Linnaeus: an owl with ear-tufts of six feathers, vol. 1, part 2, p. 288.

Bochart's conjecture is confirmed by the testimony of Bar Bahlul, the Syro-Arabic lexicographer, who, as Castell reports in the Heptaglot, renders the Syriac ܟܘܟܒܝ by the Arabic البوم الطيطي [al-būm al-ṭīṭī]. The first of these words means little owl, as we saw in the preceding Chapter; the second, which I could find in no lexicon, I interpret as spotted, from the Chaldee טִיט, so that a spotted little owl is meant. There are indeed several species of little owl marked with white or ash-grey spots.

What Russell has about the شاهين [shāhīn] in the Natural History of the city of Aleppo p. 68 deserves to be added here: „For bird-hawking, they use a large falcon, with long legs, somewhat like the goshawk, which they call espeer; and two smaller falcons, stiled the one Zanous, and the other shaheen. This latter must be taken out of the nest, for when old they cannot be trained, and is so fierce, that it will fly at ang thing. If there were not several gentlemen now in England, who can attest it, I should scarce ventnre to mention, that with the shaheen, which is about the size of a pigeon, they often take the largest eagles, of which in this country there are plenty. They formerly were trained to seize the eagle under the wing: and so depriving him of the use of that part, they fell to the ground together: but their present method, as I am informed, is to seize him on the back between the two wings, which has the same effect, but brings him down more slowly, and so gives the falconer time, to come in to his hawk's assistance; in which if he is not very expeditious, the hawk is in either case speedily destroyed.“

But J. D. Michaelis, in Supplemm. ad Lexx. vol. 5, p. 1692, thinks it probable that the little owl, if it is indeed the Hebrew תנשמת, took its name from breathing, since certain species of little owls are accustomed at some season of the year to draw mournful breaths and gasps from deep in the chest. Yet Michaelis leans more towards the opinion he put forward in the hundredth Question proposed to those about to travel to Arabia by order of the King of Denmark, p. 328, that תנשמת is the goose, to which he thinks the name was given from נשם, breathing, because this bird, when angry, stretches out its neck and hisses at whatever it takes for an enemy. To the objection someone might raise, that the Jews do not count the goose among the unclean birds, he tries to reply that the traditions of the Jews about the meaning of Hebrew words deserve no credence, and that they permit many things contrary to the Law and have accepted them in daily use. According to the spirit of the Mosaic law on unclean foods, he says, the eating of no animal, not even the pig, should have been forbidden more than that of the goose, which is very unwholesome and especially fosters skin diseases. He said more in Mosaic Law vol. 4, §. 203, pp. 198—200, and §. 205, pp. 214–215. — To Oedmann (in the Vermischt. Sammlung, part 3, ch. 5, p. 50 ff.) תנשמת is the Pelecanus Onocrotalus of Linnaeus (vol. 1, part 2, p. 569), to which he thinks the name was given from breathing no less than to the lizard chameleon (see above, vol. 2, p. 505 of our edition). For just as this lizard swells up by drawing in air, so in the Pelecanus onocrotalus too the very large, capacious and wrinkled pouch that hangs beneath the lower mandible is easily dilated by breathing, so that its capacity is astonishing. To this argument, drawn from etymology, Oedmann added another (p. 52 ff.): that it is scarcely credible that Moses should have passed over in silence, in the food laws, a bird so common in Egypt and Eretz Yisrael, and not forbidden it to the tables of the Jews, since the bird is a voracious eater of fish and has tough flesh with an almost unbearable smell, especially when older. — You see, reader, that all these opinions, like Bochart's own, rest on etymologies; among them, however, Oedmann's seems to me more probable than the rest. But nobody could easily say anything certain about the bird תנשמת, since nothing but its name occurs in the sacred Codex.
